title: A very narrow bridge
hook: Rebbe Nachman: the whole world is a very narrow bridge, and the main thing is not to be afraid

segments.voice: Yesterday: cheshbon, an accounting, and a tailor who turned the ledger both ways on Yom Kippur.

Arms around shoulders at a Jewish wedding, a summer camp, a youth group: a roomful of people swaying to a slow Hebrew song. Kol ha-olam kulo, gesher tzar me'od. The whole world is a very narrow bridge. And the main thing is not to be afraid at all. The tune is easy to learn. The source takes a little more digging: a Hasidic master who died young, who wrote openly about sadness, and whose actual words are a little different from the song.
screen: `ARMS AROUND SHOULDERS, SWAYING.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD IS A NARROW BRIDGE.` → `WHERE DO THE WORDS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Rebbe Nachman of Breslov was, the tradition says, a great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov, whose stories you've been hearing. He lived in Ukraine and died young, in the town of Uman. His student Nathan wrote down his teachings in a book called Likutei Moharan. In one passage, Rebbe Nachman says, roughly: know that a person has to cross a very, very narrow bridge, and the rule and the main thing is not to frighten yourself at all. Much later, a songwriter turned that into the song, and changed it a little on the way. The song makes the whole world the bridge, and says, don't be afraid. The original is subtler. Some readers point to the form of the Hebrew verb, which can be heard as reflexive: don't make yourself afraid. Fear may come; standing over a drop, it usually does. What you can refuse is to feed it, to stand there frightening yourself with every way you might fall. Notice what the teaching doesn't say. It doesn't say the bridge is wide, or that you won't wobble. The path really is narrow, and you still have to cross it. His teachings speak openly about sadness and heaviness of spirit, and he also taught that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always. Not because life is easy, but because joy is how you keep walking. So the bridge isn't a promise of safety. It's permission to be scared and move anyway.
screen: `NACHMAN OF BRESLOV, IN UMAN.` · `A VERY, VERY NARROW BRIDGE.` · `DON'T MAKE YOURSELF AFRAID.` · `SCARED, AND WALKING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `NOT AFRAID AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been avoiding because it scares you: a phone call, a doctor's appointment, an apology, a conversation. Don't try to stop the fear; just notice when you start frightening yourself with stories about how it'll go, and picture only the first step, one plank, not the whole bridge. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to take it.
Rebbe Nachman, whose picture of life was a very narrow bridge: the way across is narrow, and the main thing is not to make yourself afraid.
Your line: not afraid at all. Fear may come; you don't have to feed it. That's day three hundred two.

howItsDone: The song Kol ha-olam kulo, set to Rebbe Nachman's words, is sung at weddings, camps, memorials and gatherings; Breslov Hasidim study his teachings in Likutei Moharan.

fork.setup: you're halfway across a very narrow bridge and fear rises. what does Rebbe Nachman's teaching ask?
options: turn back until the fear is gone.
don't feed the fear. keep walking.
fork.reveal: his verb can be read reflexively: don't make yourself afraid. fear may come, but you don't have to frighten yourself further.

original.note: Hebrew: a very narrow bridge, from Rebbe Nachman's teaching in Likutei Moharan.

what it means: life is narrow and wobbly, and you cross it anyway without feeding your fear.
what a scholar hears: Likutei Moharan II:48 uses the verb form yitpached, which some read reflexively, don't frighten yourself, and speaks of a person crossing, not the whole world being the bridge.

sources.work: Likutei Moharan (Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, recorded by Nathan of Nemirov)

notes: Likutei Moharan II:48 paraphrased: 'a person must cross a very, very narrow bridge, and the rule and main thing is not to frighten oneself at all' (lo yitpached klal). Confirm reference and the reflexive reading.
The song is usually credited to Baruch Chait (1970s); the script says only 'a songwriter' and 'nearly two hundred years later'. Confirm.
Nachman's dates (1772–1810), death in Uman, and descent from the Baal Shem Tov (through his mother Feiga) to confirm.
'It is a great mitzvah to be joyful always' paraphrases Likutei Moharan II:24.
